name: Karl Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, technology firms, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl Schmidt, 27, and I lead a four-person line crew for the electricity company. Yesterday we replaced a cracked crossarm above a narrow lane; I checked the isolation, climbed with Marta, and spent longer getting a safe traffic gap than tightening the hardware. I like leaving a house with lights on again, but the night callouts can knock the next day sideways.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has your path into this work been like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a two-year technical diploma and came up through the crew. I got the lead role early because I'm good at spotting a bad setup before anybody climbs, though I still ask the older hands when the ground or weather looks odd. I live with my partner Lena, who works at a bakery, and we have no children. My pay is good for this work, and we've put away more than six months of expenses; there are other utilities and contractors within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew something plain. A quicker form is fine, but the pole still has to be tested by a person who can answer for it. Our dispatch notes are often repeated twice, so I can see a little help there. I wouldn't make a speech about a software upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm more bothered by callout fatigue than by a modest AI tool. Lena and I have savings, and my lead pay isn't riding on how fast I type a report. I do wonder whether the office will use a saved hour as an excuse to leave a vacancy open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the same crew and check the new report tool against our paper job notes when the company rolls it out. In the first year I'd ask our dispatcher which entries it fills automatically, then sign only what I've checked. I'd still put a fixed amount into savings each payday because night work isn't guaranteed forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of irritation about another screen at the end of a shift. I can pay the bills if things carry on like this, and the work still needs careful hands. The fatigue is real even in a quiet future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last late callout do to your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fuse failed just before midnight on Thursday, and I slept through the breakfast Lena had made before her bakery shift. I wasn't frightened about money; I was cross that I nearly missed a loose strap on the truck the next morning. I asked Marta to do the second walk-round with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an office vacancy. Would you speak up about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operations manager what happened to the vacancy at our monthly safety meeting. If dispatch is short, crews wait longer for a clear switching order, and that's more than an office inconvenience. I wouldn't pretend a quicker form settles that question.

say: I would welcome **faster reports** if a qualified lineworker still checks the pole and signs the job.
I would ask whether a dispatch **vacancy** stays open when the paperwork gets quicker.
think: My **lead pay** rests mainly on field judgment, so a small software change does not threaten our bills.
I worry that fewer dispatch staff could slow the **switching orders** our crew needs.
do: Keep **leading** the four-person crew on repair and replacement jobs this year.
Check the **report tool** against job notes before signing its entries.
Transfer a fixed amount to **savings** each payday while callout income holds.
feel: I feel **calm** about income, though night work and extra screens still wear on me.
S0.quote: A quicker form is fine, but the pole still has to be tested by a person who can answer for it.
fieldNote: Karl links a minor software change to **accountability** at the pole, where he already leads safety decisions.
His current **savings** and lead wage make this future comfortable, while callout fatigue remains a concrete pressure.

steps.text: Keep leading the four-person line crew on repair jobs
Transfer a fixed amount from each payday into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planners and dispatchers need a seat at the table before software starts writing their schedules. Out on the road, I'd use a better fault map if the switching order has still been cleared by somebody accountable. I wouldn't tell an apprentice that a robot can do a climb just because it can make a drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours should hold for a while, but I don't know what happens to our office colleagues or Lena's bakery orders if customers lose jobs. The company could turn quicker planning into more jobs per crew, and I'm already tired after storm weeks. I have a cushion, yet I don't want a wage built on skipping checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety manager to trial the fault map with our crew and keep a log of wrong locations for three months. I'd learn the tool once the dispatcher shows how it's verified, then use it on routine routes, not blind on emergency calls. In the first year of the change, I'd take the contract supervisor's number and compare nearby employers' callout rules in case our targets get foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my own work and genuinely worried for people at desks. There are still poles, wires and weather, so I expect paid field work. What nags me is getting told to do six calls in the time we used to do four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a wrong location in your log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a street name on the dispatch sheet sent us two lanes away from the downed wire. I'd write down the actual pole number, the suggested one and the minutes lost, then give dispatch a copy. A bad map isn't just inconvenient when a live wire is involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound open to the map but wary of the targets. How would you handle that with your boss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show our manager the time lost on the bad routes and the checks that still took the same time. I'd be direct, and I'd take the supervisor's number if the answer was simply to hurry. I can afford a change of employer more easily than some of the crew.

say: I would insist that **dispatch staff** help test planning software before crews rely on its routes.
I would keep **safety checks** in place even if software makes the work list longer.
think: My field hours look **steady** for now, but higher targets could make storm work more tiring and less safe.
I worry about **office colleagues** and whether lost customer income might cut bakery demand for Lena.
do: Trial the **fault map** with dispatch and record wrong pole locations for three months.
Learn how dispatch verifies **AI routes** before using them on routine calls.
Compare nearby employers’ **callout rules** if management raises crew targets.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about pace and colleagues, though I expect to keep earning on line repairs.
S1.quote: A bad map isn't just inconvenient when a live wire is involved.
fieldNote: Karl wants proof from **pole numbers** and travel time before changing how his crew navigates live faults.
His willingness to contact a **contract supervisor** rests on nearby jobs and a savings cushion, not blind faith in a safer industry.

steps.text: Trial the fault map with dispatch on routine routes
Compare callout rules at nearby utility contractors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 could swallow dispatch, planning and a lot of my reports, but it can't yet climb our damaged poles. I'd be straight that the robots around 2031 change the field side too. Nobody should sign an isolation just because a machine drafted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 29, I'd still have hands-on work for perhaps three years after the thinking system arrives, but I wouldn't call that security for life. By 2031 I'd be 32, and a capable robot could take even the awkward climbs that earned me this lead role. Our savings buy time; they don't buy another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop counting overtime in our regular budget and move that difference into savings each month. I'd ask our technical college about a funded protection-testing course, the work that checks relays and safe switching, and enroll if the course has real equipment time. In 2029, after the thinking AI arrives, I'd keep taking paid line shifts while applying for trainee testing posts; I wouldn't wait until robots are on the trucks in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still make a list and act on it. I don't think we'd be evicted next month, but I'd lie awake thinking about making a new start at 32. The speed is the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense changes if overtime drops out of your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be the weekend trips Lena and I take by train; the rent and groceries stay covered by base pay. I'd tell Lena I want six months without treating storm callouts as spending money. She knows that money is variable already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the college before paying for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether students actually test relays and how many graduates get paid placements. A neat certificate alone doesn't convince me. If that path is crowded because AI handles much of the checking too, I'd ask the nearby contractors about field inspection work and apply there instead.

say: I would tell the crew that **planning** could change in 2028 and capable field robots could arrive around 2031.
I would refuse to sign a machine-drafted **isolation** without a responsible person checking it.
think: My hands-on role may last until **2031**, when I would be 32 and capable robots could do climbs.
Our **savings** give us breathing room, but the lead role I earned might disappear.
do: Remove **overtime** from the household budget now and save the difference each month.
Enroll in **protection testing** if the college offers funded training with equipment time.
Apply for paid **testing posts** in 2029 while still working line shifts.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short path from AI planning to robot field work, though I can still act.
S2.quote: Our savings buy time; they don't buy another trade.
fieldNote: The two-year warning makes Karl separate **thinking work** in 2028 from robot field work around 2031.
He links his 2029 **applications** to paid work, refusing to treat a certificate as proof of a job.

steps.text: Move unused storm-callout pay into savings each month
Enroll in funded protection-testing training if it includes equipment practice
Apply for paid testing posts during 2029
Keep taking paid line shifts while applications are open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us train apprentices properly instead of dumping a new manual on them. AI could handle switching plans by 2031, but the line crew should still inspect the site and challenge a bad plan. The robots around 2034 are the point when I'd ask how many human crews the company intends to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32 when the thinking AI arrives and 35 when the capable robots arrive. That's enough time to try protection testing, yet I can't assume that desk checking will survive a system that thinks better than us. I'd rather be competent in several field tasks than bet our home on one certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask the training officer to put me on relay testing alongside the normal line rota, provided it doesn't cost us our savings. I'd set aside one Saturday a month to shadow the substation crew and keep a record of the equipment I've actually handled. In 2032 I'd still take line shifts, but I'd apply for field inspection openings with contractors as the robot date gets closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less cornered than in the two-year picture. Five years gives Lena and me time to discuss work, rent and whether we want children before a robot crew is realistic. I still wouldn't take on a larger mortgage just because today's pay looks good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on that first Saturday at the substation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the testing rig, not just a slide show, and ask who checks a relay result before power goes back on. If the work turns out to be mainly reading a screen, I'll know AI could eat that part too. I'd write down what hands-on judgment remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do possible children enter this decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I have talked about a child someday, without setting a date. I'd tell her I want to see whether I can get paid inspection work before we make that commitment. I wouldn't ask her to carry all the bills while I experiment with training.

say: I would use the **five-year warning** to train apprentices and check AI switching plans at real sites.
I would press the company for a **crew forecast** before capable robots reach field work around 2034.
think: At **35**, I might face robots that can climb, so one new certificate cannot guarantee income.
I want several **field skills** because pure desk checking may go when thinking AI arrives in 2031.
do: Shadow the **substation crew** monthly and record which relay tasks require hands-on judgment.
Join **relay testing** training if the company covers costs without draining our savings.
Apply for **field inspection** roles in 2032 while continuing paid line shifts.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough warning to prepare but too little certainty to make a larger housing commitment.
S3.quote: I'd rather be competent in several field tasks than bet our home on one certificate.
fieldNote: Karl uses the longer warning to test **hands-on skills**, not to assume technical desk work will remain safe.
His tentative family plans make **housing debt** feel risky even though he currently has substantial savings and other employers nearby.

steps.text: Join company-funded relay training if equipment practice is included
Apply for contractor field inspection openings in 2032
Continue paid line shifts through the transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentices there's time to finish their hours and learn every safe way to do the job. Thinking AI by 2036 would change design and switching records, and robots around 2039 could do the climb. I wouldn't ask a young person to build a whole life on today's crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 when thinking AI arrives, I'd probably still be leading field work, and at 40 the robots could end that easy assumption. Ten years is a proper chance to build experience in substation maintenance or inspection, though neither is guaranteed safe once the machines are fully capable. I'd also want Lena's bakery work in our planning; a smart ordering system could change her hours well before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the line crew and start a yearly review of our savings, rent and skills with Lena each November. Over the next two years I'd take the company's substation maintenance rotation if a place opens, and I'd keep the relay log I mentioned. In 2037, after thinking AI arrives, I'd compare paid field roles across the local utilities and apply for whichever still needs human inspection; by 2039 I'd have to judge the robots on actual work, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened tonight. A decade lets us decide whether to have a child and build a bigger cushion without racing. I still feel sad at the thought of the climb becoming something I only describe to a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena put on that yearly review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd list base pay, her bakery hours, our savings balance and any course that led to actual paid work. I'd leave overtime out of the safe number, the way I said in the fast picture. We could make a child decision with the real figures in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you a 2039 robot really replaces a crew member?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it restore power safely in rain, on an old pole with poor records, under the same checks we face. A polished trial on a clean training yard wouldn't settle my job. If it truly does the hard jobs, I'll use the years I've had to find another paid place rather than claim the old work belongs to me.

say: I would tell apprentices to finish their **hours** while learning how AI changes switching records.
I would avoid promising that today’s **crew size** will survive field robots around 2039.
think: I expect field work to last beyond **2036**, though capable robots around 2039 could remove the lead role.
Lena’s **bakery hours** might change earlier, so our household plan needs both incomes.
do: Review **base pay**, bakery hours, savings and paid training with Lena every November.
Take a **substation rotation** if a company place opens in the next two years.
Apply for **human inspection** posts in 2037 after comparing local utilities.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the eventual loss of climbing work, but a decade gives our household room to decide.
S4.quote: A polished trial on a clean training yard wouldn't settle my job.
fieldNote: A decade changes Karl’s timetable: **yearly reviews** replace emergency budgeting, and a company rotation becomes plausible.
He still names both the **2036** thinking change and the 2039 field robot, with no claim of permanent safety.

steps.text: Keep leading the line crew while completing annual household reviews
Take a company substation maintenance rotation if a place opens
Apply for paid human inspection posts in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I can face a bad storm with a crew and a switching order, but two years to sort out a second career is short. What would help is a company-funded place doing real relay work, clear dates for any crew changes, and paid openings I can apply for while I still have line shifts. I don't want a promise that everything will be fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we owe the apprentices if we see this coming. I'd tell them honestly which field skills still earn wages and let them try the testing rig, even if that makes them better candidates than me. A good lead shouldn't hide the map from the apprentices behind the crew.

headlineQuote: A good lead shouldn't hide the map from the apprentices behind the crew.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old lineworker** leading a four-person electricity crew after a technical diploma and an unusually early promotion.
He and his partner Lena have **substantial savings**, two incomes, no children and several nearby employers.
He trusts **field evidence** and safe switching procedures, while accepting new tools after crews have checked them.
The fast AGI date brings **alarm**; longer warnings let him seek paid field training and compare employers.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** gives Karl only two years before thinking work changes and about five before capable robots reach his climbs.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **funded relay training** with real equipment time and paid openings he can apply for while still working.
He also wants **clear crew dates** from the company rather than a broad promise of security.
